summary: Flame in Freefall is a web dashboard that helps researchers and engineers find which of the 24 microgravity combustion investigations in NASA's Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) repository answer a specific fire-safety question for crewed exploration. Users pick a scenario (Moon habitat, smoke detection, suppression, material selection, model validation) and the dashboard ranks the investigations with transparent, adjustable weights and explains each ranking. Its centerpiece is an oxygen-by-pressure map of every per-test point recorded in the PSI tables, shown against the expected Moon-habitat conditions (30% O2 or more at 10.2 psi or less). The map shows where evidence is thin: among solid-fuel tests with oxygen recorded per test, none ran at 30% O2 or more, and none of FLEX's 24 droplet tests at 30% O2 or more was also at 10.2 psi or lower. Every figure traces to a PSI table, with DOIs and data-quality flags. A built-in assistant answers questions from the dataset, cites PSI IDs, and says when the data cannot answer.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

Flame in Freefall turns decades of NASA microgravity combustion experiments into decisions. It ranks, compares and interprets the 24 combustion investigations in NASA's PSI repository (19 flight investigations and 5 ground studies that reuse flight data) for crewed-exploration fire safety.

HOW IT WORKS

- Scenario ranking: choose Lunar habitat, Smoke detection, Fire suppression, Material selection or Model validation. Investigations are re-ranked with adjustable weights, and each shows a score breakdown and a radar profile.

- Moon-habitat evidence map: an O2-by-pressure chart of every per-test point in the PSI experimental tables, with the Moon-habitat zone (30% O2 or more and 10.2 psi or less, from the challenge brief), a spacesuit reference (100% O2, 4.3 psi) and Earth. Normal and inverse flames are distinguished, because an inverse flame's O2 is the burner's oxidizer flow, not the cabin atmosphere.

- Coverage by fuel phase, compare view, data-quality badges and a gaps panel (no partial-gravity data in PSI yet; rocket and propellant fires out of scope).

- An assistant answers questions grounded in the dataset, cites PSI IDs, and says when the data cannot answer. We graded it on a 20-question set that includes trap questions.

KEY FINDINGS (from the PSI tables)

- Among solid-fuel tests with oxygen recorded per test, none ran at 30% O2 or more; the highest start condition is 22.2% (BASS-II).

- FLEX has 24 tests at 30% O2 or more, none also at 10.2 psi or lower (17 sit between 10.33 and 10.50 psi).

- Only 20 chamber-atmosphere tests (all ACME CFI-G gas flames) meet both Moon-habitat thresholds.

- For 20 of the 24 investigations, the PSI tables don't record per-test oxygen and pressure together, so the data to answer the Moon question mostly isn't there.

METHOD AND HONESTY

Pressure conversions, counts and DOIs come from PSI records and are recomputed independently in tests. Defective source cells were excluded and listed, and places where PSI tables and text disagree are flagged, not hidden. Two of the six scoring dimensions come from documented rules; the other four are team judgment and labeled as a heuristic, not a NASA metric.

BENEFITS

It helps fire-safety engineers and modelers see which experiments already cover Moon-habitat conditions and where new tests (such as the upcoming partial-gravity experiments) are needed. Fine-water-mist extinguishers, smoke detection and firefighter gear show how this research also benefits fire safety on Earth.

TOOLS

HTML, CSS and vanilla JavaScript (no frameworks); Python and Node scripts that fetch and extract PSI data; a Vercel serverless function for the assistant; GitHub for the code. Code: https://github.com/chry607/nasa-space-apps

USE OF SUPER INTELLIGENCE (SI)

We used Claude (Anthropic) to write and debug the code, to write the data-extraction and test scripts, to analyze the PSI data, to review the work and to help design the interface. The in-app assistant is powered by Claude through a server function and is restricted to answering from the dataset. SI-assisted code and analysis were reviewed by the team, and the numbers were independently recomputed in tests. No images, audio or video were generated by SI, and no NASA branding is used.
